ta-l1d40q4-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the fourth question of Distinction 40 turns to reprobation and announces two articles: what it is, and whether God is the cause of hardening and blinding, which in a way correspond to reprobation.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e109.summary: First argument that reprobation adds nothing to foreknowledge. Reprobation is of evils, of which God has only knowledge of simple awareness (Dist. 38).
claims: God knows evils only by simple knowledge.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e112.summary: Second argument. What adds something to a common term does not take the common name, as a convertible not indicating substance takes the name 'proper' (property) because it adds nothing, as a definition does; reprobation takes the name of foreknowledge, since we call the wicked foreknown and the good predestined.
claims: The reprobate are called 'foreknown'.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e115.summary: Third argument. In Dist. 35 Lombard gave the concepts of what adds to foreknowledge (disposition, providence, and so on) and did not mention reprobation.
claims: Lombard omitted reprobation.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e119.summary: Sed contra. Foreknowledge is of goods and evils, but reprobation is only of the damned.
claims: Reprobation is narrower than foreknowledge.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e122.summary: Second sed contra. Reprobation is opposed to approbation, which is something in the will, and opposites belong to the same thing.
claims: Reprobation involves will.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e125.summary: Thomas's determination. Reprobation adds to foreknowledge the character of providence. Divine providence is of all, but in a special, privileged way of those with will, by which they are capable of eternal glory, ordering them to the end and conferring what promotes it. Since such a nature can fail to attain the end, providence has ordered that such failure yield to the good of justice, punishment being applied to fault. So as providence regarding the good of attaining grace and glory, with foreknowledge of the outcome, is predestination, providence regarding the opposite evil, with foreknowledge of the failure, is reprobation. Since good falls under providence as caused and ordered, predestination is the cause of the grace and glory it is ordered to; since evil falls under it not as intended or caused but only as foreknown and ordered, reprobation is only foreknowledge of fault, not its cause, but foreknowledge and cause of the punishment by which the fault is ordered.
claims: Reprobation is providence regarding failure, with foreknowledge of it.
Reprobation foreknows fault without causing it, and foreknows and causes the punishment that orders it.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e128.summary: Reply to the first argument. Of evils as they occur God has knowledge of simple awareness, but as they are ordered he also has knowledge of approbation, which the name 'reprobation' implies.
claims: God approves the ordering of evils.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e131.summary: Reply to the second argument. Reprobation adds nothing to foreknowledge on the side of the reprobate, since nothing is caused in him by which he becomes evil, so it takes the common name; but it adds something on the side of God reprobating, the will of ordering punishment to fault. So in the abstract it takes the common name less than in the concrete: the reprobate is called foreknown more than reprobation is called foreknowledge.
claims: Reprobation adds the will to order punishment, nothing in the reprobate.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e134.summary: Reply to the third argument. Reprobation is opposed to predestination, so it is understood through its opposite, predestination, which was mentioned.
claims: Reprobation is understood through predestination.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e146.summary: First argument that God causes hardening and blinding. 2 Cor. 4:4 says 'the god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers', and a Gloss expounds it of the true God.
claims: God blinds unbelievers.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e152.summary: Second argument. Blinding and hardening are just punishments, and every just punishment is from God.
claims: Just punishments are from God.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e155.summary: Third argument. If affirmation causes affirmation, negation causes negation (Posterior Analytics), and God's willing causes someone's having grace, so his not willing causes someone's lacking grace, which is hardening.
claims: God's not willing causes lack of grace.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e159.summary: Fourth argument. What by its presence causes a ship's safety, the pilot, by its absence causes its danger (Physics 2), and God by his presence in the soul causes grace.
claims: God's absence causes hardening.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e162.summary: Sed contra. The saints (Dionysius, Augustine, Anselm) say someone lacks grace because he would not receive it, not because God would not give it, since he offers his light to all, though not all receive it, as the blind do not receive the sun's light.
claims: Lack of grace is from refusal to receive.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e165.summary: Second sed contra. No one is blamed or punished for what he does not cause, and people are blamed and punished for hardening or lack of grace.
claims: Blame requires causation.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e168.summary: Thomas's determination. Hardening sometimes means the act of a will obstinate in evil, pertinaciously adhering to it, and then man, not God, is its cause, as of any sinful act as deformed. Sometimes it means the privation of grace, also called blinding, since grace is a light of the soul and a perfection enabling it to good. Lacking grace happens because the person will not receive it or because God does not or will not infuse it, and the second holds only on supposition of the first: God wills only good, and lacking grace is not good simply, so absolutely God does not will it; but it is good that one lack grace if he will not have it or prepares negligently, since this is just, and so God wills it. So the first cause of this defect absolutely is on the side of the person; on God's side there is a cause only on supposition of the human cause. In this way God is sometimes called the cause of blinding or hardening, not by infusing malice but by not imparting grace, which is in his power, since if he does not impart grace necessarily, not imparting is in his power, so he is in some way the cause of not imparting. This defect, like any other, arises from the defect of a secondary cause, not the first, though God does not prevent it, as he could, lest he impede nature. Compared to the will as proximate cause, the will has causality toward it, not accepting the good offered when it could, and so is culpable, since evil whose principle is the will is such. Compared to God, it is not caused by him but only permitted and ordered, so that the will's failing is its own punishment (Augustine, Confessions 1: 'you have commanded, Lord, and so it is, that every disordered mind is its own punishment'), and this ordering is from God. So God has no causality toward the defect, only toward its ordering, which is meant when he is said to harden.
claims: Hardening as obstinate will is caused by man; as privation of grace, its first cause is the person's refusal.
God hardens only by not imparting grace on supposition of refusal, permitting and ordering the defect as punishment.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e174.summary: This answers the first argument. Some say God causes hardening as nature causes rest, which is plainly false, since natural rest is the end of natural motion intended per se by nature, which cannot be said here; rather God is said to blind by permitting the defect and ordering it.
claims: God blinds by permitting and ordering, not as nature causes rest.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e177.summary: Reply to the second argument. Hardening is called a punishment as a defect already ordered, and so it reduces to divine causality by reason of the order, which is from God, not of the defect.
claims: Hardening as punishment is from God by its order, not its defect.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e181.summary: Reply to the third argument. An effect follows only when all causes concur, and the failure of one yields its negation. God is the cause of grace as agent and the soul as recipient, as subject and matter; matter or subject does not cause the form induced unless the accident flows from its principles, which grace does not, so the soul is not simply called the cause of grace but only recipient, God the cause. Not every defect arises from the agent; it can arise from the recipient, as here.
claims: Lack of grace can arise from the recipient, not the agent.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e184.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. God in himself is absent to no one, but man absents himself from the present God, as one who closes his eyes from present light, so the comparison fails.
claims: God is never absent; man absents himself.

ta-l1d40q4-d1e193.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'Understanding the implicit condition makes truth in the dictum and impossibility in the true': of two dicta, 'Peter can be damned' (true) and 'Peter cannot be damned' (false), adding the condition implied in 'predestined' makes the false true (if Peter is predestined, he cannot be damned) and the true impossible, impossibility referring to necessity of consequence. (2) Lombard's opponents deny this 'in the actions or operations of God and of men'. God's operations are those he performs with no creature mediating, like understanding and willing, measured by eternity, not time, so they do not take on the necessity of the past but remain in the freedom of the present, without loss of immobility (God cannot will now and later not will what he now wills, but his eternal willing is always in his will's freedom), so no necessity follows from predestination's truth on the side of the predestiner, any more than of the predestined, since he can predestine and not predestine. Operations of God and men are those God performs through or in a creature, which, measured by time on the creature's side, pass into the past and acquire necessity. (3) 'Thus hardening seems in a way an effect of eternal reprobation' adds 'in a way' because reprobation is not simply the cause of hardening but only of its permission and ordering.
claims: Conditional necessity follows from predestination, not absolute.
Immanent divine operations remain free, unlike operations through creatures that become past.

ta-l1d40q4-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces two articles on reprobation: what it is and whether God causes hardening and blinding.

ta-l1d40q4-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 holds that reprobation adds to foreknowledge the character of providence regarding failure: God foreknows the fault without causing it and wills to order punishment to it, which he causes. Nothing is caused in the reprobate by reprobation, and it is understood as the opposite of predestination.
claims: Reprobation foreknows fault and wills its punishment, causing only the punishment.

ta-l1d40q4-Dd1e138.summary: Article 2 holds that hardening, as obstinate will, is caused by man. As privation of grace, its first cause is the person's refusal to receive grace offered to all. God hardens only by not imparting grace on supposition of that refusal, permitting and ordering the defect as its own punishment. Lack of grace arises from the recipient, and God is never absent; man absents himself.
claims: God hardens only by permitting and ordering, not by causing the defect.

ta-l1d40q4-Dd1e188.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 40 explains the conditional necessity implied by 'predestined' and the freedom of immanent divine operations measured by eternity. It glosses hardening as 'in a way' an effect of reprobation, which causes only its permission and ordering.
claims: Predestination implies only conditional necessity.

ta-l1d40q4.summary: Quaestio 4 of Book I, Distinction 40 treats reprobation. Article 1 holds that reprobation is providence regarding failure: it foreknows fault without causing it and wills and causes the punishment that orders it. Article 2 holds that hardening and blinding have their first cause in the person's refusal of grace, and that God hardens only by not imparting grace on that supposition, permitting the defect and ordering it as punishment.
claims: Reprobation causes punishment, not fault.
God permits and orders hardening, whose cause is human refusal.
